niche.intro: Eight niches are listed below because they work for Filipino remote professionals right now — in 2026. But "right now" always changes. New niches emerge, old ones saturate, AI reshapes what actually pays. The list below will eventually go stale. The rubric that produced it won't.
niche.creed: A list of 8 niches is a snapshot. The ability to evaluate any niche is permanent.
niche.examplesNote: The 8 niches below are worked examples of this rubric, already scored against real 2026 demand. Study *why* each one lands where it does — then run the same seven questions on a niche we never listed. That's the actual skill.

criteria.name: Real demand
criteria.question: Are there live job posts for this — this week?
criteria.why: A niche can look perfect on paper and still have nobody hiring for it. Demand overrides every other good answer — no live openings means no clients, no matter how much you'd enjoy the work.

criteria.name: Pay ceiling
criteria.question: What do the top people in this niche actually earn?
criteria.why: Starting pay tells you what's true today. The ceiling tells you if it's worth three years of your life — some niches top out fast, others keep paying more the longer you're in them.

criteria.name: Barrier to entry
criteria.question: Can I be credible to a client in 90 days?
criteria.why: A niche you can't credibly enter for a year isn't wrong — it just isn't your first niche. You need income while you're still learning, so pick something you can prove within a season.

criteria.name: Competition
criteria.question: How many other people can do this as well as I can?
criteria.why: If ten thousand people can do exactly what you do, clients pick on price — and price wars favor whoever's desperate, not whoever's good. Low competition, or a real way to stand out, protects your rate.

criteria.name: Fit
criteria.question: Would I still choose this on a bad day?
criteria.why: Pay and demand get you hired. Fit gets you to year two. The niches that burn people out are usually the ones picked for the pay band alone, not because the daily work actually suited them.

criteria.name: Durability
criteria.question: Is AI or automation eating this job in the next 3 years?
criteria.why: Some niches are one task an AI model can already do in a single prompt — those are shrinking fast. Others need judgment, relationships, or representing a business, which stay harder to automate. Bet on the second kind.

criteria.name: Transferability
criteria.question: Do these skills carry to a better role or niche later?
criteria.why: If this niche doesn't work out, or you outgrow it, do the skills open other doors? A niche that teaches you nothing transferable is a dead end even while it's still paying well.

howToResearch.title: Run a live job-post audit
howToResearch.desc: Search Indeed, OnlineJobs.ph, Upwork, and LinkedIn for the niche's actual job title. Filter to posted this week. If nothing is live right now, the niche isn't in demand today — no matter what a course or a YouTube video claims.

howToResearch.title: Read 20 real listings, not 2
howToResearch.desc: Two listings show you nothing — twenty show you the pattern: the tools every client mentions, the years of experience they ask for, the tasks that repeat. That pattern is the real job description. Write it down.

howToResearch.title: Study 5 senior profiles
howToResearch.desc: Find 5 people already doing this niche for 2+ years, on LinkedIn, Upwork, or a Facebook group. What do they charge now versus when they started? What did they add along the way to get there? That's your real pay ceiling and your roadmap.

howToResearch.title: Stress-test it against AI
howToResearch.desc: Search "[niche] AI replace 2026" and deliberately read sources that disagree with each other, not three that agree with you. If the job is "do a task a model can now do in one prompt," the ceiling is falling. If it's "judge, decide, or represent a business," it holds up longer.

howToResearch.title: Run the bad-day test on yourself
howToResearch.desc: Picture your worst week: an annoying client, low energy, still three hours of work left. Would you still rather be doing this than any other niche on your shortlist? If the honest answer is no, fit is broken — no matter how good the pay band looks on paper.

equipment.intro: The tier lists on this page (a ₱9,000 laptop, a ₱1,300/mo internet plan) are reference points for where the bar sits today — not shopping instructions. What actually decides whether a spec is worth paying for is a short list of physics and failure points, not marketing copy. Learn it once and you'll never overpay for a laptop, a plan, or a gadget again — for this job or any other.
equipment.creed: Don't buy what a list tells you. Learn what actually matters, then buy the cheapest thing that clears the bar.
equipment.referenceNote: The tiers below aren't shopping instructions — they're reference points for where the bar sits today. Use the spec literacy above to judge whether a deal, a hand-me-down, or a secondhand listing actually clears it.

whatMatters.spec: RAM and SSD — not the CPU generation on the sticker
whatMatters.whatMattersAndWhy: RAM decides how many tabs, apps, and calls you can run without freezing mid-shift. An SSD decides how fast the machine boots and opens files. Most office-work slowdowns come from running out of RAM or waiting on a slow hard drive — rarely from CPU speed.
whatMatters.howToJudge: 8GB RAM is the floor for real client work; go 16GB if you'll run design or dev tools alongside a browser and a call. Confirm it's an SSD, not an HDD — search the exact model name plus "specs" if the listing doesn't say.
whatMatters.dontOverpayFor: The newest CPU generation. A 3-generation-old i5 with 16GB RAM and an SSD will outperform a brand-new i3 with 8GB and a hard drive, for a fraction of the price.

whatMatters.spec: Upload speed and stability — not the download number on the plan
whatMatters.whatMattersAndWhy: Video calls, file uploads, and screen shares depend on upload speed. Most PH home plans advertise download speed because it's the bigger, more impressive number — but a call drops on upload, not download.
whatMatters.howToJudge: Ask your ISP for the upload speed specifically, or run a speed test and check the second number, not the first. 5 Mbps+ upload is workable for calls; 10 Mbps+ is comfortable. No drops during peak hours matters more than the top speed on the plan.
whatMatters.dontOverpayFor: A 200 Mbps plan when your actual bottleneck is your router's Wi-Fi range or a shared household connection at night. Fix stability and placement first.

whatMatters.spec: A power backup — before a better webcam
whatMatters.whatMattersAndWhy: A brownout mid-call costs more than any camera upgrade ever will: a missed deadline, a client wondering if you're reliable. Filipino remote professionals lose clients to power outages far more often than to video quality.
whatMatters.howToJudge: A basic UPS (650VA) buys 15–30 minutes to save your work and switch to mobile data — enough to finish a call gracefully. Check the runtime rating on the box, not just the price tag.
whatMatters.dontOverpayFor: A ring light or 4K webcam before you have any backup power at all. Nobody has ever lost a client over camera resolution.

whatMatters.spec: A noise-cancelling microphone — before a better camera
whatMatters.whatMattersAndWhy: Clients tolerate a soft-focus camera. They don't tolerate not being able to hear you over a barking dog, a passing jeepney, or an electric fan. Audio clarity reads as competence; video quality barely registers.
whatMatters.howToJudge: Test any headset in a noisy room before buying — record a voice memo with background noise playing and listen back. A ₱1,000 USB headset with a boom mic beats a ₱5,000 webcam for how professional you actually sound.
whatMatters.dontOverpayFor: 4K resolution or wide-angle lenses. 1080p is plenty — most clients video-call at a fraction of that resolution anyway.

whatMatters.spec: Battery health, not just the specs sheet — for anything secondhand
whatMatters.whatMattersAndWhy: A used laptop's listed specs (RAM, CPU, storage) say nothing about whether the battery still holds a charge or the charging port is loose. Those are the two things that actually fail on old laptops.
whatMatters.howToJudge: Ask the seller for a battery health screenshot (built into Windows or macOS settings) before buying — under 80% health means you're tied to an outlet for life. Test the charging port by gently wiggling the cable while it's plugged in.
whatMatters.dontOverpayFor: A "like new" claim with no battery health proof attached. Ask, every time — a good seller shows you without hesitation.

whatMatters.spec: A second monitor and ergonomic chair — real upgrades, wrong order
whatMatters.whatMattersAndWhy: These genuinely help productivity and your back over years of sitting — but they don't affect whether you get hired. They're quality-of-life upgrades, not requirements to start.
whatMatters.howToJudge: Ask yourself: would I lose a client or fail to apply without this? If no, it's a later purchase — once income is steady, not before you've landed your first client.
whatMatters.dontOverpayFor: A premium ergonomic chair or a QHD monitor in month one. Start with the ₱1,500 laptop riser and cushion setup; upgrade when your back, or your income, actually tells you to.

buyingSmart.title: Buy secondhand from the right places
buyingSmart.desc: Facebook Marketplace groups (search "laptop for sale [your city]"), Carousell, and local computer shops with a physical storefront and warranty are safer than a random online stranger. Meet in a public place with wifi so you can actually test the unit before paying — a mall, a coworking space, any Jollibee with wifi all work.

buyingSmart.title: Test before you pay — every time
buyingSmart.desc: Boot it up, open ten browser tabs plus a video call to check for lag, run a battery-health check, plug in the charger and wiggle the cable to check the port, and open a plain white window to check the screen for dead pixels or lines. Five minutes of testing saves you a ₱15,000 mistake.

buyingSmart.title: Red flags to walk away from
buyingSmart.desc: The seller won't let you test before paying. The price is far below every other listing for the same specs. They push GCash-only payment before you've seen the item in person. The serial number is scratched off or missing. Any one of these is a reason to walk, not negotiate.

buyingSmart.title: Decide upgrade-now vs. upgrade-later with one question
buyingSmart.desc: Would I lose a client, or fail to apply, without this? If yes, it's now. If the honest answer is "it would just be nicer," it's later — buy it once a real client need proves you actually require it, not because a list said so.

buyingSmart.title: The rule that saves you money forever
buyingSmart.desc: Buy the cheapest thing that clears the bar for the work you're doing today. Don't buy for the job you hope to have in a year — you can always upgrade with your first month's pay. Overbuying upfront is money you can't use to survive the gap before your first client.
